The learned Judge of the Adalat after hearing the parties rejected the said application observing that since the Directors of both the companies are same and since both the companies took loan from the same plaintiff bank there was no difficulty in disposing of the suit against the two defaulting companies. Petitioner thereupon moved the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 6477 of 2011. A Division Bench of the High Court Division disposed of the Rule with a direction upon the plaintiff-bank to amend the plaint enabling it to strike out one of the borrower companies along with the claim against such borrower. The High Court Division also directed the Artha Rin Adalat to allow amendment of the plaint in the light of the observations made in the judgment. Mr Abdul Baset Majumder, the learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the High Court Division fell into error in allowing the respondent No. 2 bank to amend the plaint by striking out the name of one of the borrower companies and the claim as against that company from the plaint and also to make further necessary amendment to the plaint. He further submits that the High Court Division failed to consider that the petitioner being aggrieved by the misjoinder of parties and the causes of action moved the petition but it gave full relief to the plaintiff despite the fact that it did not pray either in the Artha Rin Adalat or in the High Court Division for amendment of the plaint. 

 5. We have heard the learned counsel and perused the connected papers including the impugned judgment. There is no dispute that the petitioner availed of loan facility from the plaintiff-bank by mortgaging landed property and it failed to repay the loan with interest. On a plain reading of the plaint it is prima-facie found to have been drawn up on joinder of two causes of action and misjoinder of parties. The petitioner challenged the above misjoinder but by the same, it stated in paragraph 4 of the petition that the plaint does not disclose any cause of action. This claim is conflicting. On reading of the petition as a whole we find that the petitioner has admitted that the plaint discloses two causes of. 

 6. If the plaint discloses .a cause of action, the correctness or otherwise of the allegations constituting the cause of action is beyond the power of Order VII, rule 11. A plaint cannot be rejected on the ground of disclosure of two causes of action or of misjoinder of parties. If the defects for which the plaint can be rejected should not be such as are curable by amendment and nothing more than an error of procedure, the court should not reject the plaint. These may be good grounds to be agitated at the peremptory hearing of the suit but on those grounds a plaint cannot be rejected. The rejection of plaint at the threshold entails very serious consequences. This power has to be used in exceptional circumstances and ought to be used only when the court is absolutely sure that the plaintiff does not have an arguable case at all. A dismissal of suit and a rejection of plaint are not identical terms. A plaint can be rejected on any of the grounds mentioned in Order VII, rule 11 of the Code and not otherwise. The High Court Division, in the premises, committed no error of law in not rejecting the plaint.
